items.headline: IoT, AR, and Spatial Computing Need Unified UX Strategy
items.background: As products increasingly span physical and digital touchpoints — from IoT sensors to AR overlays to spatial computing interfaces — designers face the challenge of creating coherent experiences across radically different interaction paradigms. Most existing UX frameworks were built for screen-based, single-device contexts.
keyFindings: Omnichannel ecosystems require designing for simultaneous data flows across IoT, AR, and spatial layers rather than sequential user journeys
Collaborative spatial environments introduce new UX considerations around shared state, latency, and multi-user presence
AR and spatial computing demand context-aware design that adapts to physical environment variables screens don't have
items.implications: Designers working on connected product ecosystems should audit whether their current design systems account for non-screen interaction states. This is most immediately relevant to teams building enterprise tools, smart home products, or industrial applications.

items.headline: Being Data-Driven Means Choosing the Right Data First
items.background: Product teams often default to tracking whatever metrics are easiest to instrument, then struggle to extract meaningful decisions from dashboards full of noise. This piece, written in Portuguese, addresses the foundational problem of data selection before analysis.
keyFindings: Being data-driven requires deliberately selecting which data is relevant to a specific decision, not interpreting all available data
Dashboards are outputs of a data strategy, not a substitute for one
Product decisions without a defined question first lead to confirmation bias in metric interpretation
items.implications: Before instrumenting a new feature, define the decision the data needs to support. This applies especially to early-stage product teams tempted to over-instrument and under-interpret. Note: article is in Portuguese.

items.headline: The Real UX Question: What Does Good Judgment Look Like Now?
items.background: The AI-replaces-designers debate has dominated UX discourse, but it arguably distracts from a more pressing shift: if task-completion efficiency is no longer the primary UX benchmark, what is? This piece argues the profession needs to redefine its core success criteria.
keyFindings: Task completion speed as the dominant UX metric is becoming obsolete as AI handles more rote interactions
The more consequential design challenge is how to support user judgment, trust, and agency in AI-mediated systems
UX value is shifting from interaction efficiency toward outcomes like comprehension, confidence, and appropriate reliance on AI
items.implications: Practitioners should revisit how they're defining success metrics for AI-assisted features — click-through and task-time data may not capture whether users are making better decisions. Relevant to anyone designing AI-facing interfaces.

items.headline: Paper Proposes a Web-Native Rethink of the Design Canvas
items.background: Figma and similar tools treat the design canvas as a flat, file-based workspace that exports to the web. This piece proposes an alternative model where the canvas is architecturally aligned with how the web actually works, rather than abstracting away from it.
keyFindings: Current design canvases model documents, not the web's linked, stateful, and responsive nature
A web-native canvas would treat components as live web constructs rather than visual proxies for them
The gap between design canvas and browser output is the source of significant handoff friction and fidelity loss
items.implications: This is a conceptual piece rather than a product announcement, but it's useful for teams evaluating design tooling or building internal design systems — particularly those frustrated by design-to-code translation gaps.

items.headline: Zillow Cuts 91 Jobs in Washington, Senior Roles Hit Hardest
items.background: Zillow has undergone multiple rounds of restructuring since shutting down its iBuying business in 2021. This latest round of cuts in its home-state workforce continues a broader pattern of tech companies trimming senior and specialized headcount.
keyFindings: 91 employees in Washington state were laid off in this round
Senior-level roles were disproportionately affected, suggesting cost-driven restructuring rather than capability gaps
Zillow has not publicly detailed which product or design teams were affected
items.implications: For UX and product professionals in the proptech or real estate tech sector, this signals continued instability at one of the category's largest employers. Senior practitioners should note that tenure and seniority are not insulating factors in current tech layoffs.

items.headline: UX Bootcamp Ad Disguised as Editorial Content
items.background: Training program promotions frequently appear in UX content feeds dressed as editorial articles. This entry is a promotional piece for an in-person UI/UX training program in Pune, India, published on a user-contributed content platform.
keyFindings: This is a promotional listing for a UI/UX training course, not editorial or research content
The piece offers no original findings, frameworks, or data
Published on Kompasiana, an Indonesian user-generated content platform
items.implications: No actionable findings for practitioners. Included for transparency in this digest batch.

items.headline: ZoCo Design Convenes Ohio Health Leaders Around UX Challenges
items.background: Healthcare UX remains fragmented, with individual health systems and vendors often solving the same usability and workflow problems in isolation. ZoCo, a health-focused UX consultancy, hosted a convening aimed at identifying shared challenges across Ohio health organizations.
keyFindings: The event focused on identifying cross-organizational UX problems in healthcare rather than showcasing individual solutions
Participating organizations included health system leaders, suggesting buy-in at the operational level
No specific research outputs or findings have been published from the convening yet
items.implications: For UX practitioners in healthcare, this signals growing appetite for consortium-based UX research — an approach that could yield more generalizable findings than single-institution studies. Worth monitoring for published outputs.

items.headline: iF Design Opens UK Office in London
items.background: iF Design Award is one of the most recognized international design prizes, historically centered in Germany. Opening a UK representative office represents a geographic expansion of their industry presence post-Brexit.
keyFindings: iF Design has established a new representative office in London
The move extends iF's regional footprint into the UK market independently of its German headquarters
No details provided on specific programs, award submissions, or events tied to the UK office
items.implications: Minimal immediate impact for practitioners. UK-based designers and agencies seeking iF award submissions or partnerships may find local representation more accessible going forward.

items.headline: Jakob Nielsen Lists 76 Unsolved Problems in AI Usability
items.background: AI usability research is still nascent — most published work addresses narrow use cases, and there's no consensus framework for evaluating how well people can work with AI systems. Nielsen has compiled a structured list of open research questions to help orient future work in the field.
keyFindings: 76 distinct open questions are identified across categories including explainability, error recovery, trust calibration, and human-AI collaboration
Many questions address how users form and update mental models of AI behavior — an area with almost no established design guidance
The list is intended as a research agenda, making it directly applicable for teams designing AI evaluation studies
items.implications: Highly useful for UX researchers designing studies around AI-facing products — the question list functions as a gap analysis for your current research program. Also valuable for product teams trying to articulate AI-specific usability risks.

items.headline: Agentic AI Use Cases: 40+ Examples Across Industries
items.background: Agentic AI — systems that autonomously plan and execute multi-step tasks — is moving from research demos into deployed products. Understanding the practical deployment landscape helps product and UX teams anticipate where agentic patterns will affect their work.
keyFindings: Use cases span customer service automation, software development, supply chain management, healthcare triage, and financial analysis
Most real-world deployments combine a large language model with external tool access and a memory or planning layer
Enterprise adoption is currently ahead of consumer deployment, concentrated in workflow automation and decision support
items.implications: UX designers working on enterprise software should expect to encounter agentic AI features in the near term — particularly in tools involving multi-step workflows. Designing for oversight, intervention, and error recovery in autonomous task sequences will be a critical new competency.
